questions.prompt: A management fee charged on committed capital (rather than invested capital) primarily favors whom?
choices: The LPs, because they only pay on deployed capital
The GP, because it earns fees on undrawn capital too
Neither; the two bases always produce the same fee
The fund administrator
questions.explanation: A committed-capital base charges the fee on the full commitment regardless of deployment, so the GP earns on undrawn capital. Invested-capital (net invested cost) is the LP-favorable base, charged only on deployed capital.

questions.prompt: In a European (whole-fund) waterfall, when can the GP first earn carried interest?
choices: As soon as any single deal is exited at a profit
Only after all fund capital plus the whole-fund preferred return have been returned to LPs
Immediately, on the first capital call
Only after the management fee has been fully paid
questions.explanation: European waterfalls compute carry across the entire fund: no carry is paid until all contributed capital and the whole-fund pref are returned to LPs. Deal-by-deal (American) is the structure that pays carry per realized deal.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a hard hurdle from a soft hurdle?
choices: A hard hurdle has no catch-up, so the GP earns carry only on profit above the hurdle; a soft hurdle adds a catch-up so the GP eventually earns its full carry % on all profit
A hard hurdle is always higher than a soft hurdle by definition
A soft hurdle is calculated on gross profit, a hard hurdle on net profit
A hard hurdle compounds while a soft hurdle is always simple
questions.explanation: The defining difference is the catch-up. A soft hurdle (with catch-up) lets the GP eventually collect its full carry on all profit; a hard hurdle has no catch-up, so the GP's take is permanently below the stated carry %. ILPA prefers the hard hurdle.

choices: The fund returned 44% IRR
The fund underperformed the public index by 44%
The fund beat the public-index alternative (KS-PME > 1 indicates outperformance)
The fund exactly matched the public index
questions.explanation: KS-PME is a ratio of the future-valued distributions plus ending NAV over the future-valued contributions, compounded at the index. Above 1.0 means PE beat the index; below 1.0 means it lagged. It is not an annualized rate (Direct Alpha provides that).

questions.prompt: Which hurdle structure does ILPA Principles 3.0 prefer, and what does it concede about it?
choices: A soft hurdle, conceding the GP earns more than the stated carry
A hard hurdle, conceding the GP will not actually receive the full stated carry percentage
No hurdle at all, conceding LPs bear more risk
A simple (non-compounded) hurdle, conceding it is GP-favorable
questions.explanation: ILPA 3.0 prefers the hard hurdle and openly acknowledges it means the GP will not in fact receive the stated carry percentage, because there is no catch-up over the pref portion.

questions.prompt: Why does a pure deal-by-deal (American) waterfall require a robust clawback?
choices: Because management fees can exceed carry
Because the GP can be overpaid on early winners before later losers are realized
Because LPs may default on capital calls
Because the preferred return never compounds
questions.explanation: Deal-by-deal carry is paid as each deal exits. Early winners can pay the GP more carry than its true share of whole-fund profit before later losers are realized, so a clawback (often backed by escrow) trues this up at wind-up.

questions.prompt: An LP contributes $100,000,000 at t=0. With an 8% preferred return compounded annually over 5 years, what is the total preferred return amount? (dollars)
Given that 5-year, 8% compounded pref of $46,932,807.68 on $100M, what is the full 100% GP catch-up amount for a 20% carry? (dollars)
European waterfall, $100M in, $200M out over 5 years, 8% pref, 100% catch-up, 20% carry: what is the GP's total carry? (dollars)
questions.explanation: With a full catch-up at this return level, the GP ends with exactly 20% of the $100M profit = $20,000,000 (return of capital $100M + pref $46.93M + catch-up $11.73M + GP's 20% of the $41,333,990.40 residual).

questions.prompt: Same fund ($100M→$200M, 5 yr, 8% pref, 20% carry) but with a HARD hurdle (no catch-up). What is the GP's carry? (dollars)
questions.explanation: Hard hurdle: LP gets capital ($100M) + pref ($46,932,807.68); the remaining $53,067,192.32 splits 80/20, so GP = 0.20 × $53,067,192.32 = $10,613,438.46 (~10.6% of profit, roughly half the soft-hurdle result).

questions.prompt: Two-deal deal-by-deal fund: Deal A ($50M cost) returns $150M at t=3 and the GP banks $20M carry; Deal B ($50M cost) returns $20M at t=5 (a loss). Total fund profit is $70M. How much must the GP return as a clawback? (dollars)
What is the Kaplan-Schoar PME for: contributions FV $150; distributions FV $96; ending NAV FV $120?
questions.explanation: KS-PME = FV(distributions + ending NAV) / FV(contributions) = ($96 + $120) / $150 = $216 / $150 = 1.44, so PE beat the index.

questions.prompt: Walk through a standard four-tier European distribution waterfall, naming each tier in order and the split.
questions.modelAnswer: Tier 1, return of capital: 100% to LPs until all contributed capital is returned. Tier 2, preferred return: 100% to LPs until they earn the hurdle (typically 8% compounded) on that capital. Tier 3, GP catch-up: typically 100% to the GP until the GP holds its carry percentage (e.g. 20%) of all profit distributed so far, including the pref. Tier 4, carried-interest split: the residual splits 80/20 (LP/GP). The defining feature is that it is computed across the whole fund, so no carry is paid until the entire fund's capital and pref are covered.

questions.prompt: A GP markets a 9% hurdle as LP-friendly. What four things should you check before believing the optics?
questions.modelAnswer: Check (1) whether it is computed on gross or net IRR (gross is GP-favorable); (2) whether it compounds or is simple (simple accrues less, GP-favorable); (3) whether there is a full catch-up that neutralizes the hurdle at higher returns; and (4) when it starts accruing (at first call vs only after the investment period, and whether a subscription line delays capital being at risk). A 9% hurdle with gross IRR, simple accrual, a full catch-up, and a delayed start can be more GP-favorable than a plain 8% term.
